Seminar week 8 by Marc Calvo Schwarzwalder

Date: 2026-10-29 at 11am
Speaker: Marc Calvo Schwarzwalder (Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya)
Host: Kevin Morney

Title: Mathematical Modelling of Adsorption Columns State of the Art and Future Perspectives

Abstract: Column adsorption is an essential separation and purification process widely used in water treatment, greenhouse gas capture, air purification, and chromatography. While classical mathematical models for single-component systems under idealized conditions are well established, real-world applications present complex physical and chemical challenges that push standard models beyond their limitations. In this talk we provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of column adsorption modelling, focusing on recent theoretical advances that bridge the gap between simplified mathematical descriptions and realistic industrial environments. We will start from the general description for trace amounts, consisting of an advection-diffusion equation for mass transfer within the column and a kinetic equation for describing the adsorption mechanisms, and will discuss how this formulation is tweaked in different situations, such as the presence of large amounts of contaminant, consideration of multiple contaminant species to be removed simultaneously, increase of the size of the adsorbing particles, etc.

Seminar week 11 by Santiago Lamata Otín

Date: 2026-11-19 at 11am
Speaker: Santiago Lamata Otín (University of Zaragoza)
Host: David Osullivan

Title: Viral Evolution and Epidemic Spreading: The Interplay of Timescales

Abstract: Epidemic outbreaks impose a substantial burden on the health and wealth of societies. Epidemic models have long been used to understand outbreak trajectories and assess the impact of control policies over relatively short timescales. Viral evolution, however, adds another layer of complexity, particularly for rapidly evolving pathogens, whose evolutionary dynamics unfold on timescales comparable to those of epidemic spreading. In this seminar, we explore how different dimensions of viral evolution reshape epidemic dynamics. Evolution across antigenic space allows viruses to escape population immunity through the interplay between mutation and immunity timescales, thereby determining whether epidemic activity can persist as an endemic state. The structure of the underlying genotype network further shapes this evolutionary exploration and can, by itself, account for seasonal or steady patterns of endemicity. Evolution in infectivity, instead, alters the conditions for epidemic onset through the interplay between evolutionary and epidemic timescales. Importantly, this coupling also challenges conventional expectations about epidemic control. Under certain conditions, interventions can alter evolutionary dynamics in ways that lead to worse epidemic outcomes than taking no action.

References:

[1] Lamata-Otín, Santiago, et al. “Genotype networks drive oscillating endemicity and epidemic trajectories in viral evolution.” Communications Physics 8.1: 502 (2025).

[2] Lamata-Otín, Santiago, et al. “Interplay between evolutionary and epidemic time scales challenges the outcome of control policies.” Physical Review Letters, In press (arXiv preprint arXiv:2603.18801) (2026).
